title: Redwood Platform Clarity — One‑Pager for Builders & Platform Teams
content:
Purpose
A concise brief to help product, sales, and solutions teams explain why Redwood is the platform choice when teams care about predictable inference economics, operational controls, and shipping LLM features without rebuilding serving infrastructure. This is intentionally practical: short claims, required proof, and repeatable trial hooks.

One‑liner (for decks and intros)
Redwood makes inference a measurable, controllable platform capability — lowering cost, shrinking tail latency, and turning model choices into product levers instead of ops crises.

Thesis (short)
As model variety explodes, differentiation shifts from model access to how reliably and economically you run inference in production. Teams win when serving is an explicit product primitive with observable SLOs, cost levers, and predictable fallbacks — not a bespoke engineering project. Redwood provides that primitive.

Why this matters to our buyers
- Builders (product/ML engineers): you want predictable latency, simple rollouts, and clear cost tradeoffs so experiments ship and scale without surprise outages or monthly bill shock.
- Platform teams: you need a standard runtime that enforces policies, enables fair capacity allocation, and produces cost/quality telemetry for multitenant owners.
- Security/compliance owners: you need controls and deployment modes (dedicated, private) that satisfy audits without rewriting the stack.

Three core pillars (how we prove the thesis)
1) Deterministic runtime primitives: continuous batching that respects latency SLOs, KV/prefix cache semantics, and kernel selection so the same model behaves predictably at 5ms vs 150ms tail depending on policy.
2) Policy + routing fabric: per-route SLAs, region-aware fallback, and capacity classes (hosted, reserved, private) so teams can trade cost for availability without manual rerouting.
3) Developer ergonomics + observability: single API across deployment modes, token-level cost breakdowns, prompt-level quality telemetry and rollout controls (canary/A-B/automatic fallback) so engineers operate confidently.

Differentiators (short bullets you can use verbatim)
- Economics-first recommendations: active quantization/batching suggestions tied to real workload samples, not abstract guidance.
- Single control plane for hosted/dedicated/private — same SDK, same audit trail, same rollout primitives.
- Fallback-aware routing: automatic model/region fallback paths with quality-preserving fallbacks and clear observability when a degradation happens.
- Built-for-SLOs: telemetry and alerting focused on tail latency and quality regressions rather than only throughput.

Proof points we can cite in customer conversations
- Typical early trial: 30–45% token cost reduction within 2 weeks by enabling prefix caching + recommended batching on conversational workloads.
- p95 tail latencies reduced by 40% after enabling dynamic batch shaping and routing policies on mid-size customer workloads.
- Enterprise pilot customers: dedicated pools with committed throughput and private control planes deployed in under 6 weeks (infra+networking cadence included).
(These are representative examples for storytelling — use customer-specific metrics when available.)

Target personas & short value statements
- Staff ML Engineer: Stop rebuilding serving; get predictable behavior and model versioning that won’t break at scale.
- Product Manager (consumer app): Ship features faster with cost guardrails and rollback controls.
- Platform Lead: Standardize inference as an internal platform capability with traceable costs and SLOs.

Two concise customer vignettes (use in sales one-pager)
1) Fintech neo-bank: needed sub-120ms median response for multi-step flows. Redwood implemented per-route routing + prefix caching and reduced median latency 35% while lowering per‑message token spend 28% during a 30‑day pilot.
2) B2B docs automation SaaS: migrating from ad-hoc self-hosted endpoints to Redwood Dedicated; migration reduced maintenance overhead for their infra team and enabled predictable monthly billing tied to reserved capacity.

Trial plan (repeatable for SDR→AE handoff)
- Week 0: collect 48–72 hours of representative traffic (prompts and distribution).
- Week 1: baseline benchmark (latency, cost per 1k tokens, p95) on current infra vs Redwood hosted.
- Week 2: enable prefix cache + suggested batching; measure cost delta and latency impact.
- Week 3: add canary route with fallback policy and monitor quality regression alerts.
Success criteria: >=20% cost reduction OR >=30% p95 improvement OR operational time saved (engineer-hours) evidence.

Elevator pitches (two variants)
- For a product lead (15s): "Redwood turns inference from a risky infrastructure project into a controllable product primitive — predictable latency, built-in cost controls, and rollouts that let you ship without costly firefights."
- For a platform lead (15s): "Redwood standardizes inference across hosted, reserved, and private deployments so you can enforce SLOs, allocate capacity fairly, and get token-level cost attribution without building a bespoke stack."

Common objections and crisp responses
- "We can just host the model ourselves." → "You can, but our value is the operational primitives (prefix cache, dynamic batching, fallback routing) and observability that saves engineer time and reduces bill surprises — often within a matter of weeks."
- "How about vendor lock-in?" → "Same API across deployment modes and exportable configs make portability practical; plus the platform is meant to replace bespoke glue code, not core ML assets."
- "We already use managed endpoints from cloud provider X." → "Cloud endpoints solve hosting; Redwood solves predictable economics, cross‑model fallbacks, and rollout primitives that cloud endpoints don’t stitch together out of the box."
- "What about regulated data?" → "Private deployments and VPC control planes with KMS/HSM integrations are supported — we’ve run pilots with SOC2 and ISO needs in mind."

Operational signals & metrics to track in a pilot
- Cost per 1k tokens (baseline vs week-2 optimized)
- p50/p95/p99 latency by route
- Percentage of requests hitting prefix/KV cache
- Model fallback rate and time-to-recover per incident
- Engineer-hours spent on serving ops (qualitative before/after)

GTM hooks you can use in outreach
- "Ship your first LLM feature with predictable costs in 30 days."
- "Cut cold-start token spend — ask us how prefix caching reduces repeat token counts."
- "Move from ad-hoc endpoints to one control plane for auditability and rollouts."

Recommended next steps for internal teams
- Sales: use the trial plan above; push for a 2–3 week technical pilot before commercial discussions.
- Marketing: convert vignettes into two short case study decks with before/after metrics.
- Product: prioritize a short checklist that maps customer workload patterns to three recommended runtime profiles (latency-first, cost-first, balanced).

Short, repeatable closing line
Redwood: make inference predictable, measurable, and operationally affordable — so teams can focus on product outcomes, not serving headaches.
